name: Wei Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at the zinc mine, what we call a bogger, a low machine that scoops broken rock from the drawpoints and carries it to the ore pass. We go down the decline in a troop carrier at about six, have a pre-start at the crib room on level 9, and then I'm mucking out stopes most of the shift. It's hot, it's loud, and you're watching the back, the roof, all the time. I like that it takes skill to do it clean without wrecking the machine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned watching the roof. What's the part of the job that wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The heat and the rosters. My wife Amina works part-time as a nurse's aide, so when I'm on nights she's juggling Yusuf, who's 14, and Lina, who's 10, on her own. And the pay. I'm on the lower band because I came over from a smaller mine and they started me at the bottom, so we live payday to payday. Last year they trialled tele-remote boggers, where a guy sits on the surface with joysticks and screens and drives the machine from there. I watched him for a shift. It worked better than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to talking about the things that matter, like ventilation and pay. Half the AI talk at work is managers trying to sound clever. I'd probably not post anything, I'm not big online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, and the tele-remote boggers keep coming in slowly no matter what. That part isn't hype, I've seen it. But slow is something I can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd put my name down for the tele-remote training if they run it again, because once a few of the boys have done it I'd feel fine doing it too. At home we'd keep chipping at the credit card. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty normal. Maybe a bit relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until a few of the others have done the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first group always cops the problems. The software crashes, the shift times are all over the place, someone gets blamed. Let my mate Danny go first, he loves gadgets. When he says it's fine, I'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on the credit card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly school stuff and the car registration. About $3,000 right now. Amina and I have a deal that we pay $150 a fortnight off it no matter what, and so far we've stuck to it.

S0.say: He'd say it's good to get back to what matters at the mine, like ventilation and pay. He sees much of the AI talk as managers trying to sound clever.
S0.think: Things carry on, and tele-remote loaders keep coming in slowly regardless, because that part isn't hype. Slow change is something he can handle.
S0.do: Carries on working and signs up for tele-remote training once a few workmates have tried it. Keeps paying $150 a fortnight off a $3,000 credit card debt.
S0.feel: Pretty normal, maybe a bit relieved.
S0.quote: Let my mate Danny go first, he loves gadgets. When he says it's fine, I'll go.
S0.fieldNote: He separates AI hype from the tele-remote loaders he has seen working with his own eyes. He's open to change, but only after others have proven it. His $150-a-fortnight deal with his wife shows quiet discipline even with almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union has to make sure the new jobs go to the people already here, not to some contractor from the city. If the bogger moves to the surface, the guy who knows the stopes should be driving it. I'd say that at the toolbox meeting and in the union group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I think I'd be okay, if I move. Underground experience is worth something in the remote room, because you know what the rock does. The risk is if I sit on my hands and they fill the seats before me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within the first year I'd do the tele-remote course and ask for a transfer to the surface operations centre. I'd start using one of the AI apps a bit more, the one Yusuf showed me, to help me with the written tests, because my reading is slow. And we'd keep paying off the card, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous but okay. It's like changing levels, new ground, same job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the AI apps right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use one now and then, mostly to write emails to the school or check a word. It's handy. I wouldn't trust it to tell me how to scale a loose back, but for paperwork it's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys who've been underground thirty years. Ray, for one, he's 58 and he still writes his pre-start sheet in capital letters with a pencil. He'd hate the surface room. I hope the union gets him a good exit.

S1.say: He'd say the union must make sure new jobs go to people already at the mine, not outside contractors. Whoever knows the stopes should drive the machine from the surface.
S1.think: He thinks he'd be fine if he moves early, because underground experience counts in the remote room. The danger is waiting until the seats are filled.
S1.do: Does the tele-remote course within the first year and asks for a transfer to the surface operations centre. Uses an AI app more to prepare for written tests and keeps paying down the credit card.
S1.feel: A bit nervous but okay, like moving to a new level of the mine.
S1.quote: He still writes his pre-start sheet in capital letters with a pencil. He'd hate the surface room.
S1.fieldNote: In this picture he moves from waiting to acting because the change is now proven around him. His concern turns quickly to older workmates like Ray. He uses AI for paperwork but draws a firm line at safety calls underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government has to slow it down or pay for it. I'd be at the union meetings saying we need a wage guarantee while people find their feet. I'd say the owners are going to get rich off this and the miners get nothing unless we fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the remote room is gone too, if the AI can drive the bogger itself. My one plan disappears. With almost no savings and nothing else in this town, I don't know what we do in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd still do the remote course, because it might buy me a year or two of work. I'd tell Amina we stop all extras, and I'd ask my brother in the city whether there's work at his warehouse, even though that's probably robots too. Once it arrived I'd sign up for whatever support there was and go to every union action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel like I was let down halfway through doing the right thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do, and what wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me save maybe two or three thousand and finish the course. It doesn't let me change trades, because an apprenticeship takes four years. That's the bit that gets me: there's no time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf, who's 14?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to plan his life around the mine like I did. He wants to be a diesel mechanic like his uncle. I'd tell him to keep going but have a second plan. I don't even know what the second plan is.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast and government must slow it down or pay for it, with a wage guarantee while people adjust. He'd say owners will get rich unless miners fight.
S2.think: If AI can drive the loader itself, his plan of moving to the remote room disappears. With almost no savings and nothing else in town, he can't see past year two.
S2.do: Finishes the remote course in the two years before anyway and cuts all extras at home. Asks his brother about warehouse work in the city, and once it arrives signs up for support and joins union actions.
S2.feel: Scared, like being let down halfway through doing the right thing.
S2.quote: An apprenticeship takes four years. That's the bit that gets me: there's no time to do it properly.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks the one plan he had, and he feels betrayed by that. He still does the course, as a way to buy time. His worry about his son echoes his own mistake of building a life around one mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government to set up proper retraining and income support, so do it now. I'd push the union to bargain for it in our agreement before 2031. I'd be calmer saying it than with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to finish something, if I start straight away. I'd be 48. I'd probably still lose the mining job, but I might land on my feet if I'm not the last to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move to the remote room so I'm earning while I learn. Then I'd start a part-time electrical course at night, because someone has to fix and install all this gear, at least for a while. We'd keep paying the card down and try to build a month of savings by the end of year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but focused. Like the start of a long shift when you know it's going to be a hard one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wait for others to go first. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not this time. In this one, by the time others have proven it, it's too late. I'd watch what Danny does for a few months, sure, but I'd sign up for the course anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company first, there's a training fund in our agreement. If not, there are government loans for trades. I'd rather owe for a course than for groceries.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for government to set up proper retraining and income support, so it should start now. He'd push the union to bargain for it before 2031.
S3.think: Five years is enough to finish a qualification if he starts at once. He'd likely still lose the mining job at 48 but could land on his feet if he isn't last to move.
S3.do: Moves to the remote room in the first year to earn while learning, then starts a part-time night electrical course. Pays down the card and aims for a month of savings by year two, using the company training fund or a trade loan for fees.
S3.feel: Tense but focused, like the start of a hard shift.
S3.quote: I'd rather owe for a course than for groceries.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he drops his usual habit of waiting for others to go first, which he explained clearly. He'd use union-bargained training money if he could. His plan has steps and timing, unlike in the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news for workers, if we use it. The union should be planning now, and so should the government, so no mining town gets left behind. I'd be the guy at the meeting saying let's write the plan, not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough for me. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown, and I'd have a trade by then. It's still the end of mining as I know it, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote course first, then a full electrical apprenticeship over four years, part-time, maybe as a mature-age apprentice with the mine's maintenance crew. We'd build up three months of savings by year five. And I'd keep watching which jobs are still around in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Still a bit of worry, because nobody knows what 2036 really looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between five and ten years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a sprint. Ten is a plan. With ten I can do it properly, the full trade, not just a short course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Amina's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks hers lasts longer, because sick people want a person holding their hand. I hope she's right. If she is, her wage carries us through the gap while I'm an apprentice.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is good news for workers if it's used, and that the union and government should plan now so no mining town is left behind. He'd push to write the plan, not just complain.
S4.think: Ten years is enough for him: at 53, with grown kids and a new trade, he can see a way through. It's still the end of mining as he knows it.
S4.do: Takes the remote course first, then a four-year part-time electrical apprenticeship as a mature-age apprentice. Builds three months of savings by year five and watches which local jobs last.
S4.feel: Mostly okay, with some worry because nobody knows what 2036 looks like.
S4.quote: Five years is a sprint. Ten is a plan.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time turns his retraining from a rushed course into a full trade. He counts on his wife's care job lasting longer to carry the family through. His tone shifts from complaint to planning as the warning time grows.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two-year one. My whole plan is to move step by step, and that one doesn't give me any steps. What would help is a wage guarantee for a couple of years after you lose your job, and free trade courses for people our age, run at the mine, not in some city college.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if they rush robots underground and something goes wrong, it's still people who go down to fix it. Don't forget the people who'll still be underground.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but if they rush robots underground and something goes wrong, it's still people who go down to fix it.
portrait: Wei Ibrahim is a 43-year-old underground loader operator at a zinc mine, living payday to payday with his wife Amina, a part-time nurse's aide, and their two children. He supports the union and wants owners and government to share the gains, but his personal style is to wait until something is proven and then move. In the slower scenarios he plans to go from the remote control room to a full electrical trade. In the two-year AGI picture his step-by-step plan collapses, and he feels let down halfway through doing the right thing.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because his whole plan is to move step by step and it leaves him no steps.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guarantee for a couple of years after losing work, and free trade courses for people his age run at the mine rather than in a city college.
